topic: Explanation of margin of error or reliability rates for the Intoxilyzer 5000 device

rounds.text: Before administering the breath tests, Murak transported the defendant to the state police barracks in Litchfield, where he performed two tests on an Intoxilyzer 5000, yielding results of .104 and .098, respectively. Murak testified that, prior to each test, he verified the device's accuracy using a simulator solution in accordance with the regulations of the Department of Transportation. The state also called Denise Gardner, a forensic toxicologist with the Department of Public Safety's Division of Scientific Services, who explained that the Intoxilyzer 5000 determines blood alcohol content by measuring the absorption of infrared light in a sample of expired breath. She testified that the device carries a margin of error of plus or minus .003 and that its reliability rate at a .10 reading approximates 99.4 percent.

rounds.text: As a robustness check, we recompute our disruption and impact measures after removing self-citations, defined as citation links for which the citing and cited works share at least one author, inventor, or core contributor. This step addresses the possibility that teams, especially larger ones, benefit disproportionately from internal citation practices. Across papers, patents, and software repositories, the qualitative patterns remain unchanged: larger teams continue to show higher impact but lower disruption, and solo authors remain overrepresented among the most disruptive works. The correlation between team size and disruption is attenuated only slightly, and all reported differences persist in the restricted samples, indicating that our conclusions are not driven by self-citation.

The patterns do not move: larger teams still score higher on impact and lower on disruption, solo authors remain overrepresented at the top of the disruption distribution, and the team-size gradient in disruption shrinks only slightly. The conclusions in Fig. 2 therefore survive an exclusion that is, if anything, conservative for large teams.

topic: Comparison with gender or demographic composition of teams

rounds.text: A natural concern is whether the divergence between disruption and impact reflects team size itself or the changing gender and demographic composition of larger teams. Using the subset of works with author metadata, we compare disruption and top-citation impact across teams stratified by gender composition and demographic diversity (Fig. 3G). Larger teams are more gender-balanced and demographically diverse, yet the negative association between team size and disruption persists within each composition stratum, while the positive association with top-citation impact remains. These comparisons indicate that composition alone does not explain the size–disruption relationship; diverse teams are not disproportionately represented among the most disruptive works, even though they are more likely to produce highly cited work (19, 20).

rounds.text: Could the size–disruption gap simply track who is on the team? For the subset of works with author metadata, we split teams by gender composition (all-men, mixed, all-women) and by demographic diversity, then repeat the disruption and top-citation comparisons within each stratum (Fig. 3G). Teams do become more mixed as they grow. The same pattern survives inside every stratum, however: more members still predict lower disruption and higher odds of a top-citation hit. Composition does not absorb the team-size effect. Nor are diverse teams overrepresented among the most disruptive works; their advantage shows up mainly in impact, matching earlier work on team diversity and citation impact (19, 20).

topic: Legal standard or case law defining reasonable suspicion for traffic stops

rounds.text: We begin with the legal standard governing motor vehicle stops. Under the fourth amendment, a police officer may stop a motor vehicle when he has a reasonable and articulable suspicion that the operator has violated, is violating, or is about to violate the law. Terry v. Ohio, 392 U.S. 1, 21-22, 88 S. Ct. 1868, 20 L. Ed. 2d 889 (1968). Although reasonable suspicion requires more than a mere hunch, it demands considerably less than probable cause and may rest on evidence that is less reliable. State v. Aloi, 280 Conn. 824, 837-38, 911 A.2d 1086 (2007). In assessing whether such suspicion existed, we examine the totality of the circumstances, giving due weight to the training, knowledge and experience of the officer. State v. Davis, supra, 283 Conn. 295.

topic: Legal standard or case law defining reasonable suspicion for traffic stops

rounds.text: It is settled that a traffic stop is a seizure, but it is permissible when the officer possesses a reasonable and articulable suspicion that the driver has committed a traffic violation or is engaged in unlawful conduct. State v. Lamme, 216 Conn. 172, 184, 579 A.2d 484 (1990); State v. Donahue, 251 Conn. 636, 644, 742 A.2d 775 (1999). That suspicion need not amount to probable cause and may rest on the officer’s observations and rational inferences drawn in light of his training and experience. State v. Mitchell, 299 Conn. 393, 400, 9 A.3d 1274 (2010). The reasonableness of the stop is assessed objectively under the facts known to the officer at the time, without hindsight. State v. Clark, 255 Conn. 268, 279, 764 A.2d 1251 (2001).

topic: Comparison with gender or demographic composition of teams

rounds.text: Our analysis also considers the relationship between team composition and the disruptive nature of scientific contributions. To this end, we examine how the gender and demographic composition of author teams influences the impact and disruption of their research. By comparing the citation and disruption metrics of papers produced by male-led teams, female-led teams, and mixed-gender teams, we can better understand the role of team diversity in driving innovation and scientific advancement. We find that mixed-gender teams produce work that is more likely to be both impactful and disruptive, potentially indicating that a diverse range of perspectives can lead to more groundbreaking scientific discoveries. Furthermore, we observe a trend where female-led teams tend to generate work that is less likely to be highly disruptive, suggesting that current gender imbalances in scientific leadership may be limiting the potential for novel contributions to the field. These findings underline the importance of promoting gender equality in scientific research and suggest that diverse team composition can play a crucial role in driving the advancement of science.

topic: Robustness check excluding self-citations

rounds.text: To ensure the reliability of our findings, we perform a robustness check by excluding self-citations from our analysis of disruption and impact. Self-citations are references within a paper or codebase to previous work by the same authors or collaborators, and can sometimes skew the results. By removing these self-citations, we aim to isolate the true external influence of a work on the field. When analyzing the data for environmental and earth sciences journals, we observe that our conclusions regarding the divergence of impact and disruption as team size increases remain consistent (Fig. 3A). Similarly, in the GitHub dataset, after excluding self-citations, the trend of decreasing disruption with increasing team size is still evident (Fig. 3B). These results underscore the robustness of our findings and provide further evidence that smaller teams are more likely to produce highly disruptive work, while larger teams may yield more impactful, but less disruptive, contributions.

topic: Explanation of margin of error or reliability rates for the Intoxilyzer 5000 device

rounds.text: The Intoxilyzer 5000 is a widely-used breath alcohol concentration (BrAC) testing device that has been proven to be both reliable and accurate. The device is designed to provide a reliable reading within a margin of error of 0.01 g/210 L, as determined by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA). This margin of error accounts for various factors such as human error, environmental factors, and the inherent variability in human physiology. Moreover, the Intoxilyzer 5000 is regularly maintained and calibrated according to the manufacturer's guidelines to ensure its accuracy. In addition to its reliability, the device is also designed to prevent tampering and false readings through the implementation of various safeguards, such as the use of a built-in mouthpiece, a closed-loop system, and a computerized data recording system. As such, the use of the Intoxilyzer 5000 in determining the BrAC of an individual provides a scientifically reliable and accurate measure of their blood alcohol content.

topic: Legal standard or case law defining reasonable suspicion for traffic stops

rounds.text: In determining whether reasonable suspicion exists for a traffic stop, courts have long adhered to the Fourth Amendment's requirement that the police must have a particularized and objective basis for suspecting the person stopped of criminal activity. This standard, as established in the landmark case Terry v. Ohio,6 requires that the police officer's suspicion be more than just an "inchoate and unparticularized hunch." Terry, 392 U.S. at 27, 88 S.Ct. 1868. Rather, it must be based on specific, articulable facts that, considering the totality of the circumstances, would lead a reasonable police officer to conclude that criminal activity may be afoot. United States v. Cortez, 449 U.S. 411, 101 S.Ct. 690, 66 L.Ed.2d 621 (1981). The officer's assessment must be judged by whether the facts available to the officer at the moment of the stop "warrant a man of reasonable caution in the belief" that the person stopped is engaged in criminal activity. Terry, 392 U.S. at 21-22, 88 S.Ct. 1868. Thus, while the standard does not require that the officer's suspicion reach the level of probable cause, it does demand that the officer's belief be grounded in more than mere speculation or conjecture.

Terry, 392 U.S. at 27, 88 S.Ct. 1868. Instead, the suspicion must be grounded in concrete, articulable facts that, when viewed in light of the totality of the circumstances, would lead a cautious law enforcement officer to deduce that criminal activity may be occurring. United States v. Cortez, 449 U.S. 411, 101 S.Ct. 690, 66 L.Ed.2d 621 (1981). The officer's assessment must be scrutinized based on whether the information available to the officer at the time of the stop would lead a person of reasonable caution to believe that the individual stopped is involved in unlawful conduct. Terry, 392 U.S. at 21-22, 88 S.Ct. 1868. While this standard does not necessitate that the officer's suspicion rise to the level of probable cause, it does require that the officer's belief be rooted in more than mere speculation or conjecture.

topic: Budget or funding constraints that limit small agencies' ability to implement security controls

rounds.text: Officials at several agencies told us that budget constraints limited their ability to fully implement information security controls. They cited competing demands for limited resources, including maintaining mission-critical systems, and difficulties funding dedicated personnel, independent testing, and timely remediation of identified weaknesses. According to these officials, agencies prioritized controls based on risk and available funding, which could delay planned improvements. Greater use of shared services and DHS assistance could help small agencies address these resource challenges.

topic: Explanation of margin of error or reliability rates for the Intoxilyzer 5000 device

rounds.text: The record reflects testimony explaining the reliability and margin of error of the Intoxilyzer 5000. The state’s expert testified that the instrument performs an internal diagnostic check and analyzes a reference solution of known alcohol concentration during testing. If the instrument fails either check, it does not report a test result. He acknowledged that the instrument has a margin of error, but explained that this figure describes the range within which an individual measurement may vary; it does not establish that a particular result is inaccurate or that the device routinely overstates blood alcohol content. He further testified that the reference solution must produce a reading within a prescribed tolerance before testing may proceed. On the basis of these safeguards, he opined that properly administered tests yield reliable results.

rounds.text: The state also presented evidence concerning the Intoxilyzer 5000. A forensic science examiner explained that the instrument runs diagnostic checks and tests a simulator solution of known alcohol concentration before reporting a result. If either procedure falls outside the prescribed limits, no result is reported. He assigned the instrument a margin of error of plus or minus 0.01. Accordingly, a reading of 0.16 percent could reflect a blood alcohol content between 0.15 and 0.17 percent. That did not mean, he cautioned, that each reading was inaccurate by 0.01, or that the instrument necessarily exaggerated the result. The margin simply accounted for variability in measurement. As to the defendant’s tests, the simulator readings were within tolerance, and the printout disclosed no diagnostic failure. He considered the results reliable.

A result of 0.16 percent, therefore, could reflect an actual blood alcohol content between 0.15 and 0.17 percent. He rejected the suggestion that 0.01 must be subtracted from every reading. The figure describes the permissible variation in measurement, he explained, not a systematic inflation of the result. The record also contained the simulator tests accompanying the defendant’s breath samples. The solution’s known value was 0.10 percent, with an acceptable range of 0.09 to 0.11 percent, and the instrument registered 0.10 percent on both occasions. The defendant’s samples, taken several minutes apart, differed by only 0.01 percent. Nothing in those figures indicated to the expert that the instrument was operating outside its accepted limits.

topic: Robustness check excluding self-citations

rounds.text: To verify that our findings are not artifacts of self-citation, we repeat all analyses after removing citation links between a work and the prior art sharing at least one common author (19). For papers, patents, and repositories alike, we recompute disruption and all other measures on this pruned network and reestimate every statistic reported above. The patterns persist essentially unchanged across datasets: solo authors remain far more likely to produce highly disruptive work, whereas larger teams continue to concentrate on hit papers that develop established ideas, with disruption declining steadily as team size grows (Fig. S3). Excluding self-citations thus has no appreciable effect on the divergence between disruption and impact that we document.
rounds.headline: AI Generated

rounds.text: Self-citations might explain away the divergence we report; they do not. We rebuild each citation network after dropping links between a work and prior art sharing at least one author (19), then recompute disruption and every other measure from the reduced networks. In journals, solo authors remain 65% more likely to produce highly disruptive work (down from 72%), and ten-person teams still rarely disturb their field despite their edge in hit papers. Repeating the exercise for patents and the 26,900-repository GitHub network gives the same result (Fig. S3): disruption and impact diverge at every team size, and no field's average disruption percentile moves by more than three positions. Authors citing their own work do not manufacture the pattern.

rounds.text: We reach the same conclusion when we strip out self-citations, a plausible confound given that teams frequently build on their own earlier work. Following standard practice (19), we drop every citation link joining a work to prior art that shares at least one author; this removes 11.3% of links among papers, 8.7% among patents, and only 4.2% among repositories, where programmers seldom fork their own code. Recomputing disruption, hit rates, and the sleeping beauty index on the trimmed network, we find the numbers barely move (Fig. S3A—C): solo authors remain 72% more likely than five-person teams to land in the top 5% disruption, ten-person teams still lead on hit papers, and disruption percentile still falls with team size. Self-citations do not drive the result.

topic: Legal standard or case law defining reasonable suspicion for traffic stops

rounds.text: Although a traffic stop constitutes a seizure for constitutional purposes, the police may briefly detain a motorist on the basis of reasonable and articulable suspicion that criminal activity has occurred or is imminent. State v. Clark, 255 Conn. 268, 283, 761 A.2d 768 (2000). The suspicion must be founded on specific facts that, considered together with the rational inferences drawn from them, justify the intrusion; an unparticularized hunch will not suffice. We evaluate those facts objectively and under the totality of the circumstances, rather than according to the officer’s subjective characterization of the encounter. State v. Donahue, 251 Conn. 636, 643, 742 A.2d 775 (1999). This standard demands less than probable cause, but it nevertheless requires a particularized basis for connecting the detained person or vehicle with the suspected unlawful conduct.

rounds.text: The principles governing reasonable suspicion are well settled. An officer may stop a vehicle when specific, articulable facts, together with the rational inferences to be drawn from them, suggest that criminal activity may be afoot. State v. Clark, 255 Conn. 268, 283, 761 A.2d 768 (2000). That determination is made objectively, on the basis of what the officer knew at the time, and not by tallying each observation as though it stood alone. State v. Donahue, 251 Conn. 636, 643, 742 A.2d 775 (1999). Facts equally compatible with lawful conduct may still contribute to the assessment. State v. Oquendo, 223 Conn. 635, 654, 613 A.2d 1300 (1992). Probable cause is not required. A hunch will not do.

rounds.text: The stop itself requires a lesser showing than the arrest that may follow it. Police may detain a motorist briefly upon a reasonable and articulable suspicion that the person has committed, or is about to commit, an offense. State v. Donahue, 251 Conn. 636, 643, 742 A.2d 775 (1999). The officer need not eliminate every innocent explanation, and behavior that seems unremarkable by itself may take on a different cast in light of the time, place and other circumstances confronting him. See State v. Oquendo, 223 Conn. 635, 654, 613 A.2d 1300 (1992). The inquiry concerns the information available when the vehicle was stopped, not the evidence uncovered during the ensuing detention. An unparticularized hunch will not suffice. The observed conduct, however, need not itself establish probable cause.

Using author names matched to gender probabilities (19), we compute for each team the fraction of women and the associated Blau diversity index, restricting attention to papers where the inferred gender of at least 90% of members is known with confidence greater than 0.85.
